(a) Definitions.—In this section:
        (1) Source provision.—The term “source provision” means a provision of law that is replaced by a title 51 provision. 
        (2) Title 51 provision.—The term “title 51 provision” means a provision of title 51, United States Code, that is enacted by section 3.  
    (b) Cutoff Date.—The title 51 provisions replace certain provisions of law enacted on or before July 1, 2009. If a law enacted after that date amends or repeals a source provision, that law is deemed to amend or repeal, as the case may be, the corresponding title 51 provision. If a law enacted after that date is otherwise inconsistent with a title 51 provision or a provision of this Act, that law supersedes the title 51 provision or provision of this Act to the extent of the inconsistency. 
    (c) Original Date of Enactment Unchanged.—For purposes of determining whether one provision of law supersedes another based on enactment later in time, a title 51 provision is deemed to have been enacted on the date of enactment of the corresponding source provision. 
    (d) References to Title 51 Provisions.—A reference to a title 51 provision is deemed to refer to the corresponding source provision. 
    (e) References to Source Provisions.—A reference to a source provision, including a reference in a regulation, order, or other law, is deemed to refer to the corresponding title 51 provision. 
    (f) Regulations, Orders, and Other Administrative Actions.—A regulation, order, or other administrative action in effect under a source provision continues in effect under the corresponding title 51 provision. 
    (g) Actions Taken and Offenses Committed.—An action taken or an offense committed under a source provision is deemed to have been taken or committed under the corresponding title 51 provision.

fable.w: This is a transitional and savings provision for the codification of title 51; it only sets out how source provisions, references, and prior actions carry over to the new title. The tempting reading is that the mention of a "regulation, order, or other administrative action" signals rulemaking, but the text merely continues existing regulations in effect and grants no new authority to issue rules. No party outside the federal government is consulted, heard, or given a right to sue over any federal decision.
fable.s: A regulation, order, or other administrative action in effect under a source provision continues in effect under the corresponding title 51 provision.

qwen_block.w: This section consists entirely of technical definitions and rules of construction regarding the codification of laws into Title 51 of the U.S. Code. It does not establish any process for consultation, public comment, advisory boards, or coordination with outside parties. It merely clarifies how references to old and new statutory provisions should be interpreted.
qwen_block.s: (a) Definitions.—In this section: (1) Source provision.—The term “source provision” means a provision of law that is replaced by a title 51 provision. (2) Title 51 provision.—The term “title 51 provision” means a provision of title 51, United States Code, that is enacted by section 3.

opus.w: This section only manages the move of existing laws into title 51: definitions, a cutoff date, which law wins when they conflict, cross-references, and carrying over existing regulations and actions. The mention of regulations in subsection (f) only keeps existing ones in force. It doesn't authorize new rulemaking or require any comment period, hearing, or consultation, so no one outside the federal government takes part in a federal decision.
opus.s: A regulation, order, or other administrative action in effect under a source provision continues in effect under the corresponding title 51 provision.
opus.b: 1. **Tempting reading:** Subsection (f) mentions "Regulations, Orders, and Other Administrative Actions," which can look like a grant of rulemaking power. It isn't one. It only says that regulations already in force under the old provisions stay in force under the new title 51 numbering. It doesn't authorize any new rulemaking, comment period, hearing, or consultation. The whole section is standard housekeeping for moving laws into a new title, and no one outside the federal government plays any part in a federal decision.

qwen_chat.w: This section deals with the technical codification of laws, specifically how provisions from previous laws ('source provisions') are treated when moved to Title 51 of the U.S. Code. It states that existing regulations and orders continue in effect, but it does not create any new requirement for public participation, consultation with outside entities, or advisory committees. The mention of 'regulations' is descriptive of their legal status, not prescriptive of a participatory process.
qwen_chat.s: (f) Regulations, Orders, and Other Administrative Actions.—A regulation, order, or other administrative action in effect under a source provision continues in effect under the corresponding title 51 provision.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that because the section mentions "regulations, orders, and other administrative actions," it implies a process of rulemaking or consultation. However, this section is purely technical, dealing with the codification and continuity of laws (moving provisions from one title of the U.S. Code to another). It does not establish any new process for public input, advisory committees, or consultation with outside entities. It simply states that existing regulations remain in effect.
